title: Result: news, or background?
question: Is the outcome of a fight of his the article's news, or recalled as background?
readings: Strict: the outcome is news only when telling it is the article's job (a fight report, his bout on a results page); a statement, interview or callout after the fight has other news, and the outcome is just the occasion.

Fresh: the outcome is news whenever the article tells it as recent ('on Saturday', 'yesterday', with the method and scores), whatever the article's angle; it becomes background only once days have passed or the text marks it as a recall.
Topic: the outcome is news whenever the fight and how it ended is what the article talks about, even ten days later in an interview; it is background only when the article is about something else.
signals: Where the outcome sits in the lead sentence: as the main clause ('Donchenko won another bright fight') or tucked into a side clause ('praised Gaethje after losing', 'spoke about his fight against Soriano').
Recall markers in front of the outcome: 'Нагадаємо' (recall that), 'as a reminder', 'after his June loss', 'since the defeat'. A fresh report never introduces its own news this way.

Days between the fight date in the text and the published date: one day (778, 779, 797), six days (44), ten days (1172). The readers' 'unsure' notes name this gap on both the day-after and the ten-day pieces.

How much fight detail the body carries: method, round, scorecards, round-by-round (779 has all; 797 has scores and a judge's name; 44 has method and round; 778 has scores in one recall sentence; 1172 has it only in his own answers).
Who speaks: nobody (a results page, source no_one) points to the outcome as the news; him speaking (a statement, a cage or backstage interview) points to what he said as the news.
What the headline promises: 'bright scrap in Paris' (779) versus 'names next opponent' (778), 'first statement since defeat' (44), 'has veteran in mind' (797), a quote about Usman (1172).

rules.name: lead_clause
rules.text: Say yes only when the headline, or the main clause of the article's first sentence, states that he won or lost. Say no when the outcome sits in a side clause ('after losing', 'spoke about his win'), behind a recall marker ('as a reminder', 'since his defeat'), or only deeper in the body, however recent the fight.

examples.why: Lead main clause: 'Donchenko got another bright win'. Yes.
Lead: 'Donchenko spoke about the fight'; the win comes next behind 'Нагадаємо' (recall that). No, though the fight was yesterday.
Lead main clause: 'On 5 September Donchenko ... got a beautiful win'. Yes, even ten days on and even though the body is an interview.

rules.name: fresh_outcome
rules.text: Say yes when the text places the fight within seven days of the published date and states the outcome (who won and how) in a sentence of its own; the article's angle and recall words do not matter. Say no when the fight is older than seven days, undated, or the outcome is only a passing clause.

examples.why: Fight Saturday, published Sunday; the win with scores has its own sentence. Yes, despite 'Нагадаємо'.
Fight 5 September, published 15 September: ten days, past the window. No.

rules.name: report_only
rules.text: Say yes only when the article is a fight account: the headline or first sentence states that he won or lost, and the body tells the fight in the writer's voice (method, round, scores or round-by-round). A statement, interview or callout after a fight says no, however recent the fight and however much of it is retold.

examples.why: Round-by-round report with scores, nobody speaking. Yes.
The intro states the win, but the body is a Q&A; the fight is retold in his answers, not by the writer. No.
A callout piece; the win is one recall sentence. No.

why: It is the only rule a reader can apply from sentence shape alone, with no day count and no judgement about what the body 'is', so blind readers and a model should land on the same answer. It keeps the owner's line from #856: an outcome told as the occasion for other news is background. It costs the day-after reaction pieces: a callout article that leads with 'he spoke about the fight' says no even though the fight was yesterday (778), and that article then carries no fact at all, because a callout is a wish; the result lives in the fight report of the same claim (779). It also says yes to a ten-day-old interview whose intro restates the win (1172), which some readers will feel is stale.

per_article.44: Lead main clause is 'Topuria praised Gaethje'; the loss is in the side clause 'after losing'. No. The news is his statement and the vision loss (fact health).
per_article.778: Lead main clause is 'Donchenko spoke about the fight'; the win follows behind 'Нагадаємо'. No. The callout is a wish, so fact no_fact and firmness none.
per_article.779: Lead main clause states the win; the body is a round-by-round report. Yes, fact result.
per_article.797: Headline is the callout; lead main clause is 'Donchenko is pleased with his performance'. No. The scores sit deeper in the body. The Rodriguez callout is a wish, so fact no_fact, firmness none.
per_article.1172: Lead main clause states the 5 September win. Yes, even though the piece is an interview published ten days later; the fact stays health (the August infection is the newest thing he reveals).
